name: From Einstein to the Big Bang
description: How astronomers and physicists went from a sun-centred sky to an expanding universe with a beginning, and the instruments and ideas that got them there.

checkpoints.name: A moving Earth
checkpoints.note: An ancient Greek idea of a sun-centred sky was revived by Copernicus. Galileo and the telescope showed it was plausible, Kepler found the laws of planetary motion, and Newton explained them with universal gravitation.

checkpoints.name: Relativity and the stars
checkpoints.note: Einstein published special relativity in 1905 and general relativity in 1916. Henrietta Leavitt gave astronomers a way to measure distance, which Edwin Hubble used in the 1920s to show that the Andromeda Galaxy lies far beyond our own. Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin and Chandrasekhar worked out what stars are made of and how they end.

checkpoints.name: An expanding universe
checkpoints.note: Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies recede from us, so space itself is growing. The big bang and steady-state theories competed, dark matter was first suggested, and radio telescopes opened a new window; the cosmic microwave background settled the contest.

checkpoints.name: Pulsars and black holes
checkpoints.note: Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the pulsar PSR B1919+21 in 1967, Cygnus X-1 became a leading black hole candidate, and Vera Rubin found galaxies spin as if wrapped in unseen matter. Stephen Hawking explained such ideas to a mass audience, and the Hubble Space Telescope followed.

checkpoints.name: Ripples and first light
checkpoints.note: LIGO detected gravitational waves in 2015, confirming a prediction of general relativity, and the James Webb Space Telescope began observing in 2022, looking back at some of the earliest galaxies.
